content.intro: Learn importing data with different encodings through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Importing Data With Different Encodings matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A safe importing data with different encodings workflow separates ingestion from trusted production tables. Load into staging, validate encodings and data quality, reconcile counts, then apply well-defined changes in a transaction or restartable batch.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: UTF-8 and Unicode, Character-set mismatches, Invalid byte sequences, Locale-related number and date formats. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: UTF-8 and Unicode
items.text: UTF-8 and Unicode depends on text representation, collation, wildcard semantics, and sometimes locale. Test spaces, case, accents, Unicode, and special characters rather than assuming every database compares strings identically.

items.title: Character-set mismatches
items.text: Character-set mismatches helps break a larger query into a precise question. Check the subquery's row count and output columns, account for NULLs in membership tests, and compare the result with a simpler equivalent on a small dataset.

items.title: Invalid byte sequences
items.text: Invalid byte sequences changes how data is represented or exposed. Check dependencies, name objects consistently, keep structural changes in reviewed migrations, and rehearse the operation against a disposable copy before production.

items.title: Locale-related number and date formats
items.text: Locale-related number and date formats needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Diagnosing corrupted text
items.text: Diagnosing corrupted text depends on text representation, collation, wildcard semantics, and sometimes locale. Test spaces, case, accents, Unicode, and special characters rather than assuming every database compares strings identically.

content_blocks.expected_output: The backslash command is a psql client command, not server SQL. Confirm counts and validation results after loading; paths and permissions belong to the client machine.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
